claim: Serotonergic neurons innervating the first olfactory relay in Drosophila are inhibited by odorants.
source: Previously, we used whole-cell electrophysiology in Drosophila to show that serotonergic neurons innervating the first olfactory relay are inhibited by odorants (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: A pair of serotonergic neurons (the CSDns) innervate the antennal lobe and lateral horn.
source: A pair of serotonergic neurons (the CSDns) innervate the antennal lobe and lateral horn, which are first and second order neuropils.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the abstract and supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CSDn processes in the antennal lobe are inhibited by odors in an identity independent manner.
source: CSDn processes in the antennal lobe are inhibited by odors in an identity independent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1C-F and PCA analysis.

claim: CSDn processes in the lateral horn are excited in an odor identity dependent manner.
source: In the lateral horn, CSDn processes are excited in an odor identity dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B-C and correlation analysis in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Antennal lobe derived inhibition arises from local GABAergic inputs.
source: Using functional imaging, modeling, and EM reconstruction, we demonstrate that antennal lobe derived inhibition arises from local GABAergic inputs and acts as a means of gain control on branch-specific inputs that the CSDns receive within the lateral horn.
evidence: The claim is supported by previous work cited (Coates et al., 2017; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016) and modeling data in Figure 4.

claim: Antennal lobe inhibition acts as a means of gain control on branch-specific inputs that the CSDns receive within the lateral horn.
source: Using functional imaging, modeling, and EM reconstruction, we demonstrate that antennal lobe derived inhibition arises from local GABAergic inputs and acts as a means of gain control on branch-specific inputs that the CSDns receive within the lateral horn.
evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 4G-K and compartmental modeling in Figure 4E-F.

claim: The olfactory bulb in mammals receives a tremendous amount of centrifugal innervation.
source: For example, the olfactory bulb (OB) in mammals receives a tremendous amount of centrifugal innervation (Padmanabhan et al., 2018) that can be critical for proper olfactory behavior (Nunez-Parra et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Padmanabhan et al., 2018; Nunez-Parra et al., 2013).

claim: Centrifugal innervation of the olfactory bulb can be critical for proper olfactory behavior.
source: For example, the olfactory bulb (OB) in mammals receives a tremendous amount of centrifugal innervation (Padmanabhan et al., 2018) that can be critical for proper olfactory behavior (Nunez-Parra et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Nunez-Parra et al., 2013).

claim: Modulatory systems provide a mechanism for top-down regulation of sensory processing.
source: A prominent view of such modulatory systems is that they provide a mechanism for top-down regulation of sensory processing (Jacob and Nienborg, 2018; Thiele and Bellgrove, 2018) and help coordinate activity across brain regions (Melzer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Jacob and Nienborg, 2018; Thiele and Bellgrove, 2018).

claim: Modulatory systems help coordinate activity across brain regions.
source: A prominent view of such modulatory systems is that they provide a mechanism for top-down regulation of sensory processing (Jacob and Nienborg, 2018; Thiele and Bellgrove, 2018) and help coordinate activity across brain regions (Melzer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Melzer et al., 2012).

claim: Virtually all axons are subject to pre-synaptic regulation.
source: However, as virtually all axons are subject to pre-synaptic regulation (Miller, 1998), it is likely that most centrifugal modulatory neurons are subject to local influences by the circuits that they infiltrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Miller, 1998).

claim: Different odors can activate unique presynaptic terminals from piriform neurons that feed back into the olfactory bulb.
source: For example, different odors can activate unique presynaptic terminals from piriform neurons that feed back into the OB (Otazu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Otazu et al., 2015).

claim: The spatial pattern of cholinergic input to the olfactory bulb is odor-specific.
source: The spatial pattern of cholinergic input to the OB is also odor-specific and arises through similarly undescribed mechanisms (Rothermel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Rothermel et al., 2014).

claim: Only one serotonergic neuron per hemisphere, termed the CSDn, innervates both the first and second order olfactory neuropils in the fly brain.
source: For example, only one serotonergic neuron per hemisphere, termed the contralaterally-projecting serotonin-immunoreactive deuterocerebral neuron (CSDn), innervates both the first and second order olfactory neuropils in the fly brain (Coates et al., 2017; Dacks et al., 2006; Roy et al., 2007; Sun et al., 1993) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Coates et al., 2017; Dacks et al., 2006; Roy et al., 2007; Sun et al., 1993) and anatomical data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CSDns can be targeted genetically.
source: CSDns can be targeted genetically (Roy et al., 2007) and affect various olfactory behaviors involving appetitive (Xu et al., 2016) and pheromonal odorants, including cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA) (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Roy et al., 2007).

claim: CSDns affect various olfactory behaviors involving appetitive odorants.
source: CSDns can be targeted genetically (Roy et al., 2007) and affect various olfactory behaviors involving appetitive (Xu et al., 2016) and pheromonal odorants, including cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA) (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Xu et al., 2016).

claim: CSDns affect various olfactory behaviors involving pheromonal odorants, including cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA).
source: CSDns can be targeted genetically (Roy et al., 2007) and affect various olfactory behaviors involving appetitive (Xu et al., 2016) and pheromonal odorants, including cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA) (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Singh et al., 2013).

claim: CSDns are thought to participate in top-down modulation and to have their effects mainly in the antennal lobe.
source: The modulation of cVA-evoked behavioral responses is especially interesting because the CSDns are thought to participate in top-down modulation and to have their effects mainly in the first olfactory relay, the antennal lobe (AL) (Hill et al., 2002; Singh et al., 2013; Sun et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hill et al., 2002; Singh et al., 2013; Sun et al., 1993).

claim: CSDn processes avoid the cVA-sensitive DA1 glomerulus.
source: However, CSDn processes avoid the cVA-sensitive DA1 glomerulus (Coates et al., 2017; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016) and DA1 projection neuron (PN) odor responses are not modulated with strong CSDn stimulation (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Coates et al., 2017; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: DA1 projection neuron odor responses are not modulated with strong CSDn stimulation.
source: However, CSDn processes avoid the cVA-sensitive DA1 glomerulus (Coates et al., 2017; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016) and DA1 projection neuron (PN) odor responses are not modulated with strong CSDn stimulation (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: Whole-cell recordings show strong inhibition of the CSDn during stimulation with cVA.
source: Finally, whole-cell recordings show strong inhibition of the CSDn during stimulation with cVA (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: The CSDns express pre- and postsynaptic markers throughout their arborizations.
source: Because the CSDns express pre- and postsynaptic markers throughout their arborizations (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016), it is possible that transmitter release is locally regulated via inputs from their target networks (Gaudry, 2018) and that olfactory-mediated modulation occurs predominantly downstream of the AL.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: Nearly all compounds in a diverse panel of odorants resulted in inhibition of CSDn neurites in the antennal lobe.
source: We initially imaged CSDn neurites in the AL (Figure 1B, Figure 1—video 1) and found that nearly all compounds in a diverse panel of odorants resulted in inhibition (Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Ammonia produced a weak level of excitation in CSDn neurites in the antennal lobe.
source: The only exception was ammonia, which produced a weak level of excitation as previously reported in whole-cell somatic recordings (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1C and citation to previous work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: Inhibition in the antennal lobe scales with increasing odor intensity.
source: Inhibition in the AL scales with increasing odor intensity and the spatial pattern of activation of GABAergic LNs is odor invariant (Hong and Wilson, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Hong and Wilson, 2015).

claim: The spatial pattern of activation of GABAergic local interneurons is odor invariant.
source: Inhibition in the AL scales with increasing odor intensity and the spatial pattern of activation of GABAergic LNs is odor invariant (Hong and Wilson, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Hong and Wilson, 2015).

claim: Inhibition of the CSDn scales with odor intensity.
source: Inhibition of the CSDn also scales with odor intensity (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016), but it is unknown if unique odors can recruit distinct spatial patterns of CSDn activity within its dendrites in the AL.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: Aside from ammonia, CSDn processes in the antennal lobe receive odor-invariant inhibition.
source: Thus, aside from ammonia, CSDn processes in the AL receive odor-invariant inhibition, and this inhibition scales with odor intensity (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1F and citation to previous work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: The lateral horn is a brain region that receives direct input from the antennal lobe and mediates innate olfactory behaviors.
source: We next examined CSDn processes in the lateral horn (LH; Figure 2A), a brain region that receives direct input from the AL and mediates innate olfactory behaviors (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994).

claim: Every odorant in the panel produced excitation in the CSDn lateral horn arbors.
source: Surprisingly, we found that every odorant in our panel produced excitation in the CSDn LH arbors (Figure 2B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CSDn odor responses in the lateral horn varied spatially.
source: Furthermore, PCA revealed that CSDn odor responses in the LH varied spatially (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and displayed a greater coefficient of variation compared to responses in the AL (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2C and coefficient of variation analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: CSDn odor responses in the lateral horn displayed a greater coefficient of variation compared to responses in the antennal lobe.
source: Furthermore, PCA revealed that CSDn odor responses in the LH varied spatially (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and displayed a greater coefficient of variation compared to responses in the AL (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D (p=0.0021, Student's t-test).

claim: The processes of the CSDn have opposing responses to odor stimulation across different olfactory regions.
source: These results show that the processes of the CSDn have opposing responses to odor stimulation across different olfactory regions (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing AL and LH responses shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The CSDn has both pre- and postsynaptic sites in the lateral horn.
source: The CSDn has both pre- and postsynaptic sites in the LH (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016), so GCaMP signaling could represent either the activation of CSDn postsynaptic receptors or calcium influx at presynaptic release sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: Olfactory stimulation showed increased sytGCaMP6s signaling in CSDn lateral horn processes.
source: Olfactory stimulation showed increased sytGCaMP6s signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting odorants likely evoke transmitter release in the LH processes of the CSDn.
evidence: The claim is supported by sytGCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Odorants likely evoke transmitter release in the lateral horn processes of the CSDn.
source: Olfactory stimulation showed increased sytGCaMP6s signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting odorants likely evoke transmitter release in the LH processes of the CSDn.
evidence: The claim is inferred from sytGCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Projection neurons are a potential source of excitatory input to the CSDns in the lateral horn.
source: How might odor specific responses arise in the CSDn processes in the LH? PNs are a potential source of excitatory input to the CSDns in the LH as they are cholinergic, and their axons segregate anatomically (Jefferis et al., 2007; Tanaka et al., 2004) and functionally (Min et al., 2013; Seki et al., 2017; Strutz et al., 2014) in this region.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Jefferis et al., 2007; Tanaka et al., 2004; Min et al., 2013; Seki et al., 2017; Strutz et al., 2014) and inference from known properties of PNs.

claim: Projection neurons are cholinergic.
source: PNs are a potential source of excitatory input to the CSDns in the LH as they are cholinergic, and their axons segregate anatomically (Jefferis et al., 2007; Tanaka et al., 2004) and functionally (Min et al., 2013; Seki et al., 2017; Strutz et al., 2014) in this region.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about projection neurons.

claim: Projection neuron axons segregate anatomically in the lateral horn.
source: PNs are a potential source of excitatory input to the CSDns in the LH as they are cholinergic, and their axons segregate anatomically (Jefferis et al., 2007; Tanaka et al., 2004) and functionally (Min et al., 2013; Seki et al., 2017; Strutz et al., 2014) in this region.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Jefferis et al., 2007; Tanaka et al., 2004).

claim: Projection neuron axons segregate functionally in the lateral horn.
source: PNs are a potential source of excitatory input to the CSDns in the LH as they are cholinergic, and their axons segregate anatomically (Jefferis et al., 2007; Tanaka et al., 2004) and functionally (Min et al., 2013; Seki et al., 2017; Strutz et al., 2014) in this region.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Min et al., 2013; Seki et al., 2017; Strutz et al., 2014).

claim: The linkage distance between the spatial pattern of odor responses was highly correlated between projection neuron and CSDn responses in the lateral horn.
source: The linkage distance between the spatial pattern of odor responses was highly correlated between PN and CSDn responses in the LH (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 3C (R2 = 0.77, p=4.07*10−22).

claim: Projection neurons may provide direct synaptic input onto the CSDn locally in the lateral horn.
source: These data suggest that PNs may provide direct synaptic input onto the CSDn locally in the LH.
evidence: The claim is inferred from correlation analysis in Figure 3C and supported by GRASP data in Figure 3D-F and EM reconstruction in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Projection neurons show direct input to the CSDn throughout the lateral horn.
source: PNs from at least 17 glomeruli (presynaptic PN tracings provided as a personal communication from Greg Jefferis, Phillipp Schlegel, Alex Bates, Marta Costa, Fiona Love and Ruari Roberts) show direct input to the CSDn throughout the LH (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: The CSDns receive input from different cell classes in the antennal lobe and lateral horn to shape its olfactory responses locally.
source: Together these results suggest that the CSDns receive input from different cell classes in the AL and LH to shape its olfactory responses locally.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data on GABAergic LN input in the AL and PN input in the LH.

claim: GABAergic local interneurons constitute a major input to the CSDns in the antennal lobe and drive inhibitory responses independent of odor identity.
source: In the AL, GABAergic LNs constitute a major input to the CSDns and drive inhibitory responses independent of odor identify.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Coates et al., 2017; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016) and calcium imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Projection neurons make relatively few synaptic connections with the CSDns in the antennal lobe.
source: PNs make relatively few synaptic connections with the CSDns in the AL (Coates et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Coates et al., 2017).

claim: Olfactory responses in the CSDn neurites in the lateral horn are excitatory, odor specific, and are likely in part shaped by direct projection neuron input.
source: In the LH, olfactory responses in the CSDn neurites are excitatory, odor specific, and are likely in part shaped by direct PN input.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2, correlation analysis in Figure 3, and EM reconstruction data in Figure 3G-I.

claim: All models that displayed somatic inhibition when current was injected into the CSDn processes in the antennal lobe also showed inhibition in the lateral horn.
source: Importantly, all models that displayed somatic inhibition when current was injected into the CSDn processes in the AL also showed inhibition in the LH (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by compartmental modeling data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The geometry and passive properties of the CSDn allow the propagation of inhibition from the antennal lobe to the lateral horn during olfactory stimulation.
source: These results suggest that the geometry and passive properties of the CSDn allow the propagation of inhibition from the AL to the LH during olfactory stimulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from compartmental modeling data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The geometry of the CSDn arbors favor the propagation of voltage signals from the antennal lobe preferentially to the lateral horn.
source: This approach revealed that the geometry of the CSDn arbors favor the propagation of voltage signals from the AL preferentially to the LH (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by compartmental modeling data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Olfactory responses to all odors tested increased in the processes of the CSDn in the lateral horn following the removal of antennal lobe inhibition.
source: Olfactory responses to all odors tested increased in the processes of the CSDn in the LH following the removal of AL inhibition (Figure 4I,J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 4I-K.

claim: During normal odor sampling, inhibition from the antennal lobe propagates to suppress olfactory responses in the lateral horn.
source: These results demonstrate that during normal odor sampling, inhibition from the AL propagates to suppress olfactory responses in the LH.
evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 4I-K and compartmental modeling in Figure 4E-F.

claim: A serotonergic neuron with broad arbors integrates locally at multiple neuropil along the olfactory pathway in Drosophila.
source: Here, we show that a serotonergic neuron with broad arbors integrates locally at multiple neuropil along to the olfactory pathway in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 1-2 and laser ablation experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Synaptic inputs at the first and second order processing stages of olfaction impose opposite polarity responses in the CSDn.
source: Interestingly, synaptic inputs at the first and second order processing stages of olfaction impose opposite polarity responses in this neuron and likely decorrelate synaptic release in distinct target regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing inhibition in the AL (Figure 1) and excitation in the LH (Figure 2).

claim: Synaptic inputs at the first and second order processing stages of olfaction likely decorrelate synaptic release in distinct target regions.
source: Interestingly, synaptic inputs at the first and second order processing stages of olfaction impose opposite polarity responses in this neuron and likely decorrelate synaptic release in distinct target regions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the opposing responses in the AL and LH and the compartmental modeling showing voltage propagation.

claim: Inhibition dominates responses in the antennal lobe and odor-specific excitation is prominent in the downstream lateral horn.
source: Inhibition dominates responses in the AL and odor-specific excitation is prominent in the downstream LH.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 1-2.

claim: Across a single widely projecting modulatory neuron, branches within distinct neuropils can operate in different manners.
source: This suggests that across a single widely projecting modulatory neuron, branches within distinct neuropils can operate in different manners.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the opposing responses observed in the AL and LH of the CSDn.

claim: Invertebrate studies involving motor systems have shown compartmentalization of neurons spanning distant neuropils.
source: However, invertebrate studies involving motor systems have shown compartmentalization of neurons spanning distant neuropils (Nikitin et al., 2013; Sasaki et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Nikitin et al., 2013; Sasaki et al., 2007).

claim: The activity within a single serotonergic neuron can vary across neuropils involved in processing the same sensory modality.
source: Our results demonstrate that the activity within a single serotonergic neuron can vary across neuropils involved in processing the same sensory modality.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing different responses in the AL and LH (Figures 1-2).

claim: Local regulation of release allows modulatory functions to be employed independently in different brain regions.
source: As a given modulator may perform distinct functions in different brain regions, local regulation of release allows these functions to be employed independently.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed local integration in the CSDn and general principles of neuromodulation.

claim: Serotonin in the olfactory bulb indirectly inhibits olfactory sensory neuron terminals and has been proposed to serve a gain control function.
source: For instance, 5-HT in the OB indirectly inhibits OSN terminals and has been proposed to serve a gain control function (Petzold et al., 2009), while in the piriform cortex 5-HT has no effect on stimulus input, but rather only decreases spontaneous activity (Lottem et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Petzold et al., 2009).

claim: In the piriform cortex, serotonin has no effect on stimulus input, but rather only decreases spontaneous activity.
source: For instance, 5-HT in the OB indirectly inhibits OSN terminals and has been proposed to serve a gain control function (Petzold et al., 2009), while in the piriform cortex 5-HT has no effect on stimulus input, but rather only decreases spontaneous activity (Lottem et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Lottem et al., 2016).

claim: Serotonin has different effects on mitral cells in the main versus mitral cells in the accessory olfactory bulb.
source: Additionally, 5-HT has different effects on mitral cells in the main versus mitral cells in the accessory olfactory bulb (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Huang et al., 2017).

claim: Local regulation and decoupling of modulator release across synaptic sites has been implicated in the normal function of the mammalian dopamine system.
source: Local regulation and decoupling of modulator release across synaptic sites is not unique to invertebrates and has been implicated in the normal function of the mammalian DA system.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on dopamine release (Floresco et al., 1998; Jones et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2016; Berke, 2018).

claim: Dopamine release is only partially correlated with firing activity.
source: First, DA release is only partially correlated with firing activity, and release can be locally evoked in the absence of spiking in DA cells (Floresco et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Floresco et al., 1998).

claim: Dopamine release can be locally evoked in the absence of spiking in dopamine cells.
source: First, DA release is only partially correlated with firing activity, and release can be locally evoked in the absence of spiking in DA cells (Floresco et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Floresco et al., 1998).

claim: Local inactivation of the nucleus accumbens decreases dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens without impacting dopamine neuron firing.
source: Additionally, local inactivation of the nucleus accumbens (NA) decreases DA release in the NA without impacting DA neuron firing (Jones et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Jones et al., 2010).

claim: Dopamine release can signal both motivation and reward prediction errors on similar timescales.
source: This has led to the theory that DA release can signal both motivation and reward prediction errors (RPE) on similar timescales (Hamid et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Hamid et al., 2016).

claim: Dopamine release related to motivation is thought to be shaped by local presynaptic mechanisms.
source: Dopamine release related to motivation is thought to be shaped by local presynaptic mechanisms while dopamine related to RPE correlates more strongly with the firing properties of DA neurons (Berke, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Berke, 2018).

claim: Dopamine related to reward prediction errors correlates more strongly with the firing properties of dopamine neurons.
source: Dopamine release related to motivation is thought to be shaped by local presynaptic mechanisms while dopamine related to RPE correlates more strongly with the firing properties of DA neurons (Berke, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Berke, 2018).

claim: It is highly likely that serotonin is regulated by local presynaptic mechanisms.
source: Measuring serotonergic transmission across release sites is more difficult compared to dopamine (Dankoski and Wightman, 2013), nevertheless, it is highly likely that 5-HT is also regulated by local presynaptic mechanisms (Egashira et al., 2002; Schlicker et al., 1984; Tao and Auerbach, 1995; Threlfell et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Egashira et al., 2002; Schlicker et al., 1984; Tao and Auerbach, 1995; Threlfell et al., 2004).

claim: EM reconstructions of raphe terminals in the olfactory bulb have failed to reveal postsynaptic densities in raphe axons.
source: EM reconstructions of raphe terminals in the OB have failed to reveal postsynaptic densities in raphe axons (Gracia-Llanes et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Gracia-Llanes et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2015).

claim: Local integration in the antennal lobe and lateral horn allow the CSDn to independently process and shape sensory information at multiple points in the early olfactory pathway of the fly.
source: Local integration in the AL and LH allow the CSDn to independently process and shape sensory information at multiple points in the early olfactory pathway of the fly.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 1-2 and laser ablation experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Projection neuron axons directly excite CSDn terminals in the lateral horn in an odor specific manner while CSDn branches in the antennal lobe are inhibited.
source: Specifically, we found that PN axons directly excite CSDn terminals in the LH in an odor specific manner while CSDn branches in the AL are inhibited.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 1-2, GRASP data in Figure 3D-F, and EM reconstruction in Figure 3G-I.

claim: The CSDn soma is inhibited by odors.
source: Previous studies have shown that the CSDn soma is also inhibited by odors and that stimulation of the CSDn has little impact on olfactory circuitry in the AL (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016), despite the CSDn being critical for normal olfactory behavior (Singh et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: Stimulation of the CSDn has little impact on olfactory circuitry in the antennal lobe.
source: Previous studies have shown that the CSDn soma is also inhibited by odors and that stimulation of the CSDn has little impact on olfactory circuitry in the AL (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016), despite the CSDn being critical for normal olfactory behavior (Singh et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: The CSDn is critical for normal olfactory behavior.
source: Previous studies have shown that the CSDn soma is also inhibited by odors and that stimulation of the CSDn has little impact on olfactory circuitry in the AL (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016), despite the CSDn being critical for normal olfactory behavior (Singh et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Singh et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2016).

claim: The CSDn modulates behavior by affecting odor-processing in the lateral horn.
source: Our current study resolves this issue by suggesting instead that the CSDn modulates behavior by affecting odor-processing in the LH (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), which has previously been unexplored.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the laser ablation experiments in Figure 4 and the lack of AL modulation shown in previous work.

claim: Inhibition of CSDn processes in the antennal lobe does not appear to depend on odor identity.
source: Inhibition of CSDn processes in the AL does not appear to depend on odor identity as shown in this study, but rather correlates with the total amount of ORN activity that an odor elicits (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis in Figure 1F and citation to previous work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: Inhibition of CSDn processes in the antennal lobe correlates with the total amount of olfactory receptor neuron activity that an odor elicits.
source: Inhibition of CSDn processes in the AL does not appear to depend on odor identity as shown in this study, but rather correlates with the total amount of ORN activity that an odor elicits (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: Antennal lobe and lateral horn processes of the CSDn are electrotonically connected.
source: Our compartmental modeling shows that AL and LH processes of the CSDn are electrotonically connected, but that voltage preferentially passes from the AL to the LH.
evidence: The claim is supported by compartmental modeling data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Voltage preferentially passes from the antennal lobe to the lateral horn in the CSDn.
source: Our compartmental modeling shows that AL and LH processes of the CSDn are electrotonically connected, but that voltage preferentially passes from the AL to the LH.
evidence: The claim is supported by compartmental modeling data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CSDn inhibition scales with increasing odor strength due to robust GABAergic local interneuron input in the antennal lobe.
source: As CSDn inhibition scales with increasing odor strength due to robust GABAergic LN input in the AL (Coates et al., 2017; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016), this inhibition shunts LH responses proportionally.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Coates et al., 2017; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: Antennal lobe inhibition shunts lateral horn responses proportionally.
source: As CSDn inhibition scales with increasing odor strength due to robust GABAergic LN input in the AL (Coates et al., 2017; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016), this inhibition shunts LH responses proportionally.
evidence: The claim is inferred from compartmental modeling in Figure 4 and laser ablation experiments in Figure 4I-K.

claim: The configuration of the CSDn allows olfactory modulation to be odor specific in the lateral horn while being less dependent on odor concentration.
source: This configuration ultimately allows olfactory modulation to be odor specific in the LH while being less dependent on odor concentration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of odor-invariant AL inhibition that scales with intensity and odor-specific LH excitation.

claim: Multi-dendritic computing is critical for processing other sensory modalities, most notably vision.
source: Multi-dendritic computing is critical for processing other sensory modalities as well (Ranganathan et al., 2018), but most notably vision (Jones and Gabbiani, 2010; Koren et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Ranganathan et al., 2018; Jones and Gabbiani, 2010; Koren et al., 2017).

claim: Synaptic integration between dendrites is used to compute object motion across the visual field on a collision course with the observer.
source: Synaptic integration between dendrites is used to compute object motion across the visual field on a collision course with the observer.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about visual processing.

claim: The dendrites of starburst amacrine cells in the mammalian retina express mGluR to isolate dendritic compartments.
source: Interestingly, the dendrites of starburst amacrine cells in the mammalian retina express mGluR to isolate dendritic compartments thus preventing integration to non-preferred stimuli while enabling regulated integration specifically to preferred directions of motion (Koren et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Koren et al., 2017).

claim: CSDn neurites influence one another during olfaction.
source: Our laser ablation experiments demonstrate that CSDn neurites influence one another during olfaction, but it is intriguing that the magnitude of such coupling could be state dependent and regulated by active conductances.
evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 4I-K.

claim: The CSDn was originally proposed to participate in top-down modulation by transmitting higher order sensory information from the lateral horn to the antennal lobe.
source: The CSDn was originally proposed to participate in top-down modulation by transmitting higher order sensory information from the LH to the AL (Hill et al., 2002; Sun et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Hill et al., 2002; Sun et al., 1993).

claim: During olfaction, the CSDn acts more in a bottom-up fashion where responses in the antennal lobe have a greater impact on downstream processing in the lateral horn.
source: Our results suggest that during olfaction, the CSDn acts more in a bottom-up fashion where responses in the AL have a greater impact on downstream processing in the LH.
evidence: The claim is inferred from compartmental modeling in Figure 4F and laser ablation experiments in Figure 4I-K.

claim: Transmitter release during olfactory sampling putatively occurs only later in the sensory processing stream rather than at the earliest stages.
source: Transmitter release during olfactory sampling putatively occurs only later in the sensory processing stream rather than at the earliest stages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the inhibition in the AL and excitation in the LH, combined with sytGCaMP6s data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CSDn has numerous release sites in the antennal lobe.
source: Interestingly, the CSDn has numerous release sites in the AL (Coates et al., 2017; Sun et al., 1993; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016) and CSDn derived 5-HT directly inhibits several classes of neurons in the AL (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Coates et al., 2017; Sun et al., 1993; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: CSDn derived serotonin directly inhibits several classes of neurons in the antennal lobe.
source: Interestingly, the CSDn has numerous release sites in the AL (Coates et al., 2017; Sun et al., 1993; Zhang and Gaudry, 2016) and CSDn derived 5-HT directly inhibits several classes of neurons in the AL (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Zhang and Gaudry, 2016).

claim: It is likely that the CSDn receives input from unidentified non-olfactory sources that excite the neuron's spike initiation site allowing it to modulate in a top-down manner.
source: However, it is likely that the CSDn also receives input from unidentified non-olfactory sources that excite the neuron's spike initiation site allowing it to modulate in a top-down manner.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the presence of release sites in the AL despite olfactory inhibition.

claim: Non-olfactory stimulation of the CSDn may be consistent with top-down modulation.
source: Thus, non-olfactory stimulation of the CSDn may be consistent with top-down modulation and would constitute one mechanism by which a broadly arborizing modulatory neuron may be multifunctional depending on the source of its excitatory drive.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the discussion of potential non-olfactory inputs.

claim: Multifunctional neurons have been well described in central pattern generating networks.
source: Multifunctional neurons have been well described in central pattern generating networks (Briggman and Kristan, 2008) but are only recently becoming appreciated with regards to neuromodulation (Berke, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Briggman and Kristan, 2008).

claim: Multifunctional neurons are only recently becoming appreciated with regards to neuromodulation.
source: Multifunctional neurons have been well described in central pattern generating networks (Briggman and Kristan, 2008) but are only recently becoming appreciated with regards to neuromodulation (Berke, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work (Berke, 2018).

claim: Integration into local circuits allows modulatory cells greater flexibility in how they participate in sensory processing.
source: Our findings in Drosophila suggest that integration into local circuits allows modulatory cells greater flexibility in how they participate in sensory processing and may be a feature that is often overlooked when assessing the function of these critical components of the central nervous system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings on local integration in the CSDn.

claim: Female flies aged 3–5 weeks post-eclosion and reared at room temperature were used for experiments.
source: Female flies aged 3–5 weeks post-eclosion and reared at room temperature were used.
evidence: The claim is a methodological statement describing the experimental subjects.

claim: In vivo imaging experiments were performed at room temperature.
source: In vivo imaging experiments were performed at room temperature.
evidence: The claim is a methodological statement describing experimental conditions.

claim: 920 nm wavelength light was used to excite GCaMP6s under two-photon microscopy.
source: 920 nm wavelength light was used to excite GCaMP6s under two-photon microscopy.
evidence: The claim is a methodological statement describing imaging parameters.

claim: The CSDn was identified and partially reconstructed in the female adult fly brain dataset.
source: The CSDn was identified and partially reconstructed in the female adult fly brain (FAFB) dataset as described in Zheng et al. (2018) using CATMAID (Saalfeld et al., 2009; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016), available at https://catmaid-fafb.virtualflybrain.org.
evidence: The claim is a methodological statement supported by citations to published work (Zheng et al., 2018; Saalfeld et al., 2009; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016).

claim: A multi-compartmental conductance-based computer model of the CSDn neuron was constructed by taking its electron micrograph reconstruction and importing it into the Neuron simulator.
source: A multi-compartmental conductance-based computer model of the CSDn neuron was constructed by taking its electron micrograph reconstruction and importing it into the Neuron simulator (Carnevale and Hines, 2006).
evidence: The claim is a methodological statement supported by citation to published work (Carnevale and Hines, 2006).

claim: The variance explained by PCs 1–3 in the antennal lobe are 60.3 ± 2.2%, 6.3 ± 0.4%, and 6.1 ± 0.3%, respectively.
source: The variance and SEM explained by PCs 1–3 are 60.3 ± 2.2%, 6.3 ± 0.4%, and 6.1 ± 0.3%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The variance explained by PCs 1–3 in the lateral horn are 45.2 ± 2.6%, 12.4 ± 0.9%, and 8.6 ± 0.6%.
source: The variance and SEM explained by PCs 1–3 are 45.2 ± 2.6%, 12.4 ± 0.9%, and 8.6 ± 0.6%.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis data shown in Figure 2C.
